editorial_plan.report_thesis: The evidence supports attention to consumer-reported value sensitivities and selective spending, while treating assistant use, personalization, and human interaction at specific in-store stages as distinct experience considerations.

themes.theme: Consumers report separate hypothetical switching intentions: 74% say they would switch brands for a lower regular price elsewhere, and 71% would switch if pack sizes or product quality were reduced without clear communication; these are stated intentions, not observed switching behavior.

Self-reported impulse restraint is easing: 54% of consumers say they are making fewer impulse purchases in the current report period, down from 71% last year, a comparison the report characterizes as a modest rebound of intentional indulgence alongside persistent deal-seeking. Separately, as prices rise, around half of consumers (49%) are buying smaller quantities, which the report characterizes as consumption control rather than complete avoidance; the measurement period for this figure is not stated.

In an October 2025 survey of 12,000 consumers, reported promotion effectiveness for driving purchase decisions ranked money-off offers (e.g., $5 off $25) at 75%, percent-off offers (e.g., 20% off) at 74%, and buy-one-get-one-free offers at 73%.

Priyanka Bhargav says that today 25% of quick-commerce spending in India comes from mid- to low-affluent consumers in Tier 2 and Tier 3 towns, and that these customers are willing to pay a little extra for faster delivery.
Among consumers, 52% report using virtual assistants that automate re-ordering or meal planning at least once a week; separately, 76% want the ability to set clear rules for when an assistant acts.

Agreement among consumers surveyed with wanting Gen AI to provide hyper-personalized content and product/service recommendations based on individual preferences was 58% in November 2024 and 63% in October 2025; each survey had N=12,000 consumers.

In surveys of 12,000 consumers each, the share saying human interaction increases loyalty at the in-store customer-support stage was 54% in November 2024 and 74% in October 2025, an increase of 20 percentage points. At the in-store purchase stage, the corresponding figures were 40% and 66%, an increase of 26 percentage points.

summary.tldr: Consumers say they would switch brands for a lower regular price elsewhere (74%); separately, 71% would switch if pack sizes or product quality were reduced without clear communication.
summary.card_tldr_compact: 74% of consumers say they would switch brands for a lower regular price elsewhere.
summary.executive_summary: Consumers say they would switch brands for a lower regular price elsewhere (74%); separately, 71% would switch if pack sizes or product quality were reduced without clear communication. The report says 54% of consumers say they are making fewer impulse purchases in the current report period, down from 71% last year, and characterizes this as easing impulse restraint and a modest rebound of “intentional indulgence” alongside persistent deal-seeking. In an October 2025 survey of 12,000 consumers, money-off offers (e.g., $5 off $25) were rated most effective for driving purchase decisions (75%), followed by percent-off offers (e.g., 20% off) (74%) and buy-one-get-one-free offers (73%). Among consumers surveyed (N = 12,000 in each survey), 54% in November 2024 and 74% in October 2025 said human interaction increases loyalty at the in-store customer-support stage. MarketLense recommends assessing human interaction at the in-store customer-support stage as part of experience planning.

insights_final.text: At the in-store customer-support stage, the share of consumers saying human interaction increases loyalty was 54% in November 2024 and 74% in October 2025, an increase of 20 percentage points; each survey had N = 12,000 consumers. At the in-store purchase stage, 40% in November 2024 and 66% in October 2025 said the same, an increase of 26 percentage points; each wave had N=12,000 consumers.

expert_comment: The reported hypothetical switching conditions are distinct: 74% of consumers say they would switch brands for a lower regular price elsewhere, and 71% say they would switch if pack sizes or product quality were reduced without clear communication; neither figure measures observed switching. Separately, in an October 2025 survey of 12,000 consumers, reported promotion effectiveness for driving purchase decisions was 75% for money-off offers (e.g., $5 off $25), 74% for percent-off offers (e.g., 20% off), and 73% for buy-one-get-one-free offers. Together, these findings describe different parts of value response, not a single measure: stated willingness to switch under specified conditions sits alongside reported assessments of promotion effectiveness. When reviewing value strategy, MarketLense would recommend assessing regular-price switching sensitivity, communication of pack-size or quality reductions, and promotion effectiveness as separate decision questions.
linkedin_post:
Consumers report distinct hypothetical switching intentions under two conditions.

74% of consumers say they would switch brands if they found a lower regular price elsewhere. Consumers’ stated willingness to switch brands if pack sizes or product quality were reduced without clear communication was 71%.

These are stated intentions, not observed switching behavior. If reviewing brand value propositions, MarketLense recommends assessing regular-price positioning separately from communication about pack-size or product-quality changes.

decision_brief.strategic_context: Consumers say they would switch brands for a lower regular price elsewhere (74%); separately, 71% would switch if pack sizes or product quality were reduced without clear communication.
decision_implications: The findings capture distinct stated switching conditions, not evidence of actual brand switching.
Easing impulse restraint does not mean value pressure has lifted: the report also describes persistent deal-seeking and smaller-quantity buying as prices rise.
Treat these consumer ratings as signals of perceived purchase-decision effectiveness, not proof that one format will deliver better campaign outcomes.
priority_moves: Assess price positioning and communication about pack-size or quality changes as separate decision points.
Track impulse purchasing and quantity changes as separate value signals.
Use the reported ratings as an input when evaluating formats for purchase-decision objectives.
watchouts: The page reports that 74% of consumers say they would switch brands if they found a lower regular price elsewhere. Separately, it reports that 71% would switch if pack sizes or product quality were reduced without clear communication. Both are hypothetical stated intentions, not observed switching behavior.

When prioritizing in-store service design, assess customer-support and purchase-stage experiences separately.

claim_ledgers.claim_text: Consumers say they would switch brands for a lower regular price elsewhere (74%).
Separately, 71% of consumers would switch brands if pack sizes or product quality were reduced without clear communication.

The report says 54% of consumers say they are making fewer impulse purchases in the current report period, down from 71% last year, and characterizes this as easing impulse restraint and a modest rebound of “intentional indulgence” alongside persistent deal-seeking.

In an October 2025 survey of 12,000 consumers, money-off offers (e.g., $5 off $25) were rated most effective for driving purchase decisions (75%), followed by percent-off offers (e.g., 20% off) (74%) and buy-one-get-one-free offers (73%).
Among consumers surveyed (N = 12,000 in each survey), 54% in November 2024 and 74% in October 2025 said human interaction increases loyalty at the in-store customer-support stage.

The page reports that 74% of consumers say they would switch brands if they found a lower regular price elsewhere. Separately, it reports that 71% would switch if pack sizes or product quality were reduced without clear communication. Both are hypothetical stated intentions, not observed switching behavior.

54% of consumers say they are making fewer impulse purchases in the current report period, down from 71% last year; the report calls this easing impulse restraint and a modest rebound of “intentional indulgence” alongside persistent deal-seeking. Separately, as prices rise, around half of consumers (49%) are buying smaller quantities, which the report characterizes as consumption control rather than complete avoidance.

In an October 2025 survey of 12,000 consumers, money-off offers (e.g., $5 off $25) were rated most effective for driving purchase decisions (75%), followed by percent-off offers (e.g., 20% off) (74%) and buy-one-get-one-free offers (73%).

Priyanka Bhargav, Head of Insights and Brand Strategy at Flipkart, says that today 25% of quick-commerce spending in India comes from mid- to low-affluent consumers in Tier 2 and Tier 3 towns. She adds that these customers are willing to pay a little extra for faster delivery.
52% of consumers use virtual assistants that automate re-ordering or meal planning at least once a week. Separately, 76% want the ability to set clear rules for when an assistant acts.

Among consumers surveyed, agreement with “I want Gen AI to provide hyper-personalized content and product/service recommendations based on my individual preferences” was 58% in November 2024 and 63% in October 2025. Each survey had N=12,000 consumers.

At the in-store customer-support stage, the share of consumers saying human interaction increases loyalty was 54% in November 2024 and 74% in October 2025, an increase of 20 percentage points; each survey had N = 12,000 consumers. At the in-store purchase stage, 40% in November 2024 and 66% in October 2025 said the same, an increase of 26 percentage points; each wave had N=12,000 consumers.

report_vs/artifacts/expert_comment.public_output: The reported hypothetical switching conditions are distinct: 74% of consumers say they would switch brands for a lower regular price elsewhere, and 71% say they would switch if pack sizes or product quality were reduced without clear communication; neither figure measures observed switching. Separately, in an October 2025 survey of 12,000 consumers, reported promotion effectiveness for driving purchase decisions was 75% for money-off offers (e.g., $5 off $25), 74% for percent-off offers (e.g., 20% off), and 73% for buy-one-get-one-free offers. Together, these findings describe different parts of value response, not a single measure: stated willingness to switch under specified conditions sits alongside reported assessments of promotion effectiveness. When reviewing value strategy, MarketLense would recommend assessing regular-price switching sensitivity, communication of pack-size or quality reductions, and promotion effectiveness as separate decision questions.

source_truth_notes_by_page.24: Figure 9 directly supports the claim: the chart’s question concerns promotion effectiveness in driving purchase decisions, and the adjacent category labels pair money-off (e.g., $5 off $25) with 75%, % off (e.g., 20% off) with 74%, and BOGOF with 73%. The source line states October 2025 and N = 12,000 consumers. No geography is specified.

planned_themes: Consumers report separate hypothetical switching intentions: 74% say they would switch brands for a lower regular price elsewhere, and 71% would switch if pack sizes or product quality were reduced without clear communication; these are stated intentions, not observed switching behavior.

Self-reported impulse restraint is easing: 54% of consumers say they are making fewer impulse purchases in the current report period, down from 71% last year, a comparison the report characterizes as a modest rebound of intentional indulgence alongside persistent deal-seeking. Separately, as prices rise, around half of consumers (49%) are buying smaller quantities, which the report characterizes as consumption control rather than complete avoidance; the measurement period for this figure is not stated.

In an October 2025 survey of 12,000 consumers, reported promotion effectiveness for driving purchase decisions ranked money-off offers (e.g., $5 off $25) at 75%, percent-off offers (e.g., 20% off) at 74%, and buy-one-get-one-free offers at 73%.

Priyanka Bhargav says that today 25% of quick-commerce spending in India comes from mid- to low-affluent consumers in Tier 2 and Tier 3 towns, and that these customers are willing to pay a little extra for faster delivery.
Among consumers, 52% report using virtual assistants that automate re-ordering or meal planning at least once a week; separately, 76% want the ability to set clear rules for when an assistant acts.

Agreement among consumers surveyed with wanting Gen AI to provide hyper-personalized content and product/service recommendations based on individual preferences was 58% in November 2024 and 63% in October 2025; each survey had N=12,000 consumers.

In surveys of 12,000 consumers each, the share saying human interaction increases loyalty at the in-store customer-support stage was 54% in November 2024 and 74% in October 2025, an increase of 20 percentage points. At the in-store purchase stage, the corresponding figures were 40% and 66%, an increase of 26 percentage points.

entry.text: The executive-summary paragraph and adjacent 71% callout pair the value with consumers’ stated willingness to switch brands if pack sizes or product quality were reduced without clear communication. This directly supports the corrected claim; the page does not state the measurement period, geography, sample size, or precise denominator.

In the “Fairness and quality define value” section, the page says: “Seventy four percent of consumers say they would switch brands if they found a lower regular price elsewhere.” The nearby 71 percent figure refers instead to switching if pack sizes or product quality were reduced without clear communication, so it is not the value supporting this claim. The 74 percent statement gives no survey period, geography, sample size, or denominator.
